note: Both invocations name God as the one who conquered the five: the Kural's one who quenched the five sense-gates, Tirumular's ஐந்து வென்றனன்.

Both invocations close on the number eight: the Kural's எண்குணத்தான், one of eight qualities, and Tirumular's உணர்ந்தெட்டே. Tradition reads both as the eight divine qualities, though Tirumular's eight may also be the eightfold form.

Both make God the one with no likeness: the Kural's தனக்குவமை இல்லாதான், Tirumular's தன்னைஒப்பாய் ஒன்றும் இல்லாத் தலைமகன். The Kural adds that only reaching his feet ends the mind's anxiety; Tirumular adds that he becomes father to whoever calls him so.

The Kural asks what learning is worth if it does not bow at God's feet; Tirumular turns the test on the worshippers, saying that even those who can recite many hymns lack understanding. Bowing is necessary in one, not enough in the other.
Both rank the householder with or above the ascetic: the Kural's virtuous household life endures more than those who do penance, Tirumular's householders are equal to great ascetics.

The Naladiyar's wise, seeing the pain in pleasure, keep off the household way; Tirumular says those who stay in the household equal great ascetics. The conflict holds if 47's first line is a general claim about householders, not only those who keep the Lord in mind.

Both picture salvation as swimming a sea: the Kural's sea of births, crossed by reaching the Lord's feet, and Tirumular's sea of sin, crossed by thinking of the Lord and reaching the shore beyond pasu and pasam.
13 says the gods cannot measure the Lord; 14 states the result in a refrain, he stands beyond Brahma, beyond Vishnu and beyond everything, yet sees all.
18 has the Lord make Kubera lord of wealth for his penance and say 'take this lordship'; 19 opens on the same இதுபதி and gives another seat granted for true penance.
audit_text_issue: 19's விதுபதி may be a misreading; 18's last two lines are uncertain

note: Tirumular finds all dharma within the Veda; the Kural makes the king's just sceptre the ஆதி of both the Brahmins' books and dharma. If ஆதி is read as support they agree that the Veda needs a guardian; if read as origin, the Kural places dharma's source in rule, not in scripture.

Both separate holding the Veda from living by it. The Kural says the Veda can be relearned but lost conduct ruins a Brahmin; Tirumular complains that reciters keep the six-limbed Veda but practise none of its qualities.
Both end in நீர்மேல் எழுத்து, writing on water. 60 leaves open what is futile; 64 states the condition: Agamas without the knowledge the Lord declared.

The Kural asks what learning is worth if one does not bow at the feet of the one of pure knowledge; Tirumular says crores of Agamas are writing on water without the knowledge the Lord declared. Both measure scripture by what it leads to.

The Naladiyar says worldly books without the books of wisdom are only clamour that never removes confusion; Tirumular says even the Agamas, if their knowledge is missed, are writing on water. Both deny that bulk of learning is the point.

Both face writing beyond counting. The Naladiyar's answer is to choose what is fitting, like the bird that drinks the milk and leaves the water; Tirumular's is that the countless Agamas are hard even for the gods and their count is writing on water.
65 says the Lord spoke Sanskrit and Tamil together; 66 says what both teach, bondage, release and death, and that either leads to knowing him.
59 widens the languages of the Lord's dharma to eighteen; 66 names two, Tamil and Sanskrit. Both refuse to tie revelation to one tongue.
Both open 'by Nandi's grace' and both say Tirumular sought Mulan. 68 credits Nandi with his name and his stay in the land; 92 adds what grace did after: he became Sadasiva and entered true wisdom.

The Kural says tapas should be striven for here, since it gains what one wishes; Tirumular asks why be born again when people do not strive at tapas beforehand. Both use முயல் and place the effort now.

The Kural's learned love learning more when they see the world delighting in what delights them; Tirumular wishes the bliss he gained on the whole world. Both make a private good complete only when it is shared.
70 has the four masters told 'may you gain all that I gained'; 85 widens the same wish from four disciples to the whole world.
88 tells how Brahma and Vishnu could not find the foot and crown of the column of fire; 95 turns the same flame into the poet's own confession that he does not know its root.
69 names Kalangi among Tirumular's seven disciples; 102 makes Kalangar the head of a line through Aghorar and others, carrying the succession one generation further.
112 names one part of the Lord as the one who stands in the body and breathes; 116 makes the body a temple where Nandi has taken up residence like fire latent in bamboo.

Tirumular's third line nearly repeats the Kural's: ஒருமையுள் ஆமைபோல் ... ஐந்து அடக்கி. The Kural makes the restraint a protection through seven births (எழுமையும்); Tirumular's version ends instead with those who 'heard both' (இருமையும்) and stand flawless.
audit_text_issue: 133 இருமையுங் கேட்டு may be a corruption of கெட்டு.

note: Both use the bird that drinks milk and leaves water. The Naladiyar makes it the wise learning only what is fitting; Tirumular makes it the parting that turns deeds into seeds that cannot sprout into births.

The Naladiyar makes guarding the craving that enters through the five gates the effort that reaches release; Tirumular says the five come under control of themselves (தானே) once one has met the Lord. Restraint is a cause in one, a result in the other.
The Kural says those who reach the Lord's feet cross the sea of births; Tirumular makes the feet the refuge, the path and the goal itself.
Both call the body the Lord's temple: 116 where Nandi lives like fire in bamboo, 725 where Tirumular, who once thought the body a defect, found the Lord inside it and so tends it.

The Naladiyar calls the body a stinking cart that only the ignorant adorn and praise; Tirumular calls it the temple where the Lord dwells. The conflict holds if கோயில் is read as giving the body worth, not only as locating the Lord in it.
1924 counts the thirty-six tattvas as they unfold from bindu and nada; 126 climbs the same thirty-six as the rungs of a ladder to release.
audit_text_issue: 1924: ஐ ஐந்தும் (25) + ஆறும் (6) + ஈர்இரண்டு (4) gives 35, not ஆறுஆறு (36); a number may have dropped.

note: The Kural counts sloth and sleep among the pleasure-boats of those bound for ruin; Tirumular gives the same words (சோம்பு, தூக்கம்) to the freed resting in Sivam. The Kural's verdict is on worldly duty; Tirumular names a state beyond it.

The two verses share most of their words: the dancer in the skin bag who worked it and has left, and the indifference of what is then done to the body. Tirumular lists crows, revilers, milk drops and praisers; the Naladiyar dragging, careful burial, casting out and revilers.
Both build the body as a hut with two posts and one ridge beam. 146 says the life can't re-enter once the roof comes apart; 161 adds that it was thatched by a maker, not by ordinary thatchers.
The Kural says the world's 'greatness' is that one who was here yesterday is gone today; Tirumular shows it in a single evening: a meal, a talk with his wife, a small ache, and he is gone.

Both tell a death as a short row of ordinary acts: the Naladiyar's 'he stood, he sat, he lay down, he went', Tirumular's cooking, eating, talking and lying down. The Naladiyar draws the lesson to do good now; Tirumular draws none.
The Kural calls virtue the companion that does not perish when one perishes; Tirumular says that when the body falls only vows and knowledge go on the road with the dead, not wife or children.

Both take a king to make the point: the Naladiyar's kings under moon-white umbrellas were carried off and called dead, Tirumular's lord of the land rides a bier with the town behind and drums in front.
Both make the body a clay pot. 143 has it melt back to clay in the rain; 158 says even a broken pot is kept as shards, but a broken body is not kept a moment.
145 ends the funeral with the bath that ends remembering; 157 retells it with the kin turning back at the town's edge and calls those who bathe and leave 'people without justice'.
Both use the honey bee whose stored honey others take. The Naladiyar spells out the lesson, that those who hoard without giving lose it all; Tirumular gives only the image.

Both tell the rich to give their wealth away in view of Death, but the Naladiyar says no one has ever leapt past Death and escaped, while Tirumular says one who sheds his wealth may leap past him. The conflict holds if Tirumular's leap means escaping death; if it means dying free of fear or bondage, the two agree.
audit_text_issue: Naladiyar 6 has an encoding glitch: பிழைத்தெரிணஇ

note: Both use the phrase of leaping past Death (கூற்றம் குதித்தல்) as something attainable: the Kural through the power of austerity, Tirumular through letting go of wealth.
The two verses end with the same line (காட்டிக் கொடுத்தவர் கைவிட்ட வாறே): the bees' hoard taken by the strong, and the body left by the kin who raised it.
Both make wealth vanish without trace through a sudden image, the Naladiyar's lightning in a night cloud and Tirumular's capsizing boat; Tirumular adds a treasure in the body that does not sink.
Both read the sun's daily course as a measure of passing life: the Naladiyar urges help to others before one's days run out, Tirumular faults those who see the sun set and do not understand.
In the Naladiyar Death uses the sun as a measure to eat one's days; in Tirumular the sun and moon measure out the world from within. Both make the heavenly lights the counters of a life.

The Naladiyar says not to put off good deeds because one is young; Tirumular says to hold to Nandi while life lasts, since youth and strength wear away. The urgency is the same, the act urged differs.
The Naladiyar warns men not to desire a woman who will one day stoop over a staff; Tirumular turns the lesson on the man, who was cane to women and is now bitter fruit.
The Kural says hunger never touches one used to sharing his food; Tirumular asks for a ladleful given before each good meal, the same habit in its smallest form.

Both make shared food the right use of plenty: the Naladiyar tells one who gains wealth to eat with many from that day, since wealth turns like a cart wheel; Tirumular asks for a ladleful before one eats.
In 167 the dancer leaves the skin bag, in 189 the king leaves the drum and it turns to clay. Both make the life a performer or ruler inside an instrument that is nothing once he goes.
151 has the five who ate rice with ghee depart at death; 188 makes the five guardians of a field who abandon it when their master's summons comes.
Both say people do not understand that the sun measures out their lives, using the same verb (அளக்கின்றது) and the same complaint (அறிகிலார்).
audit_text_issue: 191 line 4 (பொன்றுணர்வாரிற் புணர்க்கின்ற மாயமே) is hard to construe

note: Both take grey hair as the sign to heed: the Naladiyar's wise renounced in childhood knowing it would come, Tirumular faults those who see black hair turn white and still do not grasp it.
Both rank not killing above ritual offering: the Kural above a thousand oblations of ghee, Tirumular as the brightest of the flowers of worship.

Both say killing is paid for after this life, but differently: the Kural through rebirth in a wretched, diseased body, Tirumular through hell; and Tirumular extends the guilt to those who only urged the killing.
Both send the flesh-eater to hell; the Kural says hell's mouth will not open to let him out, Tirumular describes his being flung into fire-mouthed hell.
Both make eating creatures a deed that returns on the eater; the Naladiyar's crab-eater gets a wasting disease in a later life, Tirumular's flesh-eater hell.
Both argue from the wife already at home: the Naladiyar asks why a man with a loving wife looks at another's, Tirumular calls it leaving ripe jackfruit for a wild date.
Both end the adulterer with a lost leg: in the Naladiyar the leg is cut off as the king's punishment if he is caught, in Tirumular he breaks it falling from the sour mango he climbed.
Both say a woman's attractive surface hides what should repel: the Naladiyar the body's foulness under the skin, Tirumular poison under fair leaves and fruit.
Both shrink the adulterer's pleasure: small against great fear in the Naladiyar, a dream and a whirlpool in Tirumular.
Both describe a woman who promises closeness and then turns away; the Naladiyar's said she would never part, Tirumular's bids the man stay near and leaves talking to others.

Both use sugarcane to show sweetness changing over time: the Naladiyar's cane eaten from the tip grows sweeter like the friendship of the learned, Tirumular's cane juice in the hand turns to neem in the body.
audit_text_issue: naladiyar:138 line 3 'துரி஢ன்தின்' contains a stray character.

note: Both say kin and dependants fall away from the poor: the Naladiyar's crows leave the carcass and no one asks 'are you well?', Tirumular's dependants turn unloving.
Both describe the poor man estranged from those closest to him; the Kural goes as far as his own mother.
Both say what can never be filled is ended not by filling it but by removing its cause: craving in the Kural, impurity in Tirumular. This depends on reading the pit as desire and not only the belly.
Both treat ties as obstacles to ending births: the Kural asks why one bent on that would keep other ties when even the body is excess, Tirumular calls clinging kin worse than deeds.
Both name the five senses as what must be overcome; the Kural says their domain must be crushed, Tirumular describes the suffering they cause until one turns to the Lord.
Tirumular praises the oblation as sustaining sky, earth and gods; the Kural ranks not killing above a thousand oblations. Read together, the rite keeps its worth but not the first place.
If புறங்கொடுத்து உண்ணுவர means eating after giving, both describe the worthy as feeding others first and eating after.
Both define the Brahmin's state by regard for every living being: the Kural's அந்தணர் are clothed in kindness to all lives, Tirumular's Brahman includes knowing all lives as one's equal.
Both define the goal by the end of craving: the Kural says the freed are those freed of craving, Tirumular that Vedanta is the place where craving ends.
Both deny that marks of the body make the holy man: the Kural says neither shaving nor long hair is needed, Tirumular that the thread is cotton and the tuft hair.
Both make the Brahmin depend on conduct, not birth: the Kural says his birth is ruined when conduct declines, Tirumular denies the name to those without truth and knowledge.
Tirumular's அந்தண்மை பூண்ட echoes the Kural's செந்தண்மை பூண்டு: both define the அந்தணர் by a coolness of heart they wear. Tirumular adds that the land where they live prospers.
If the two attachments are 'I' and 'mine', both say cutting them raises one above the gods: the Kural to a world higher than theirs, Tirumular to an offering they receive.
224 defines Brahmins by the daily rites; 232 makes the highest state one reached once the rites are set aside, so the rites are a stage, not the goal.
Both say Death does not approach the good: the Kural that it does not advance on one who keeps from killing, Tirumular that it spares the good while the unlearned king kills.
Both tie the land's prosperity to the king's conduct: the Kural rain and harvest to just rule, Tirumular the land's decline to a king who neglects austerity.
Both condemn holy garb worn without the life it stands for; Tirumular adds that the king should force such men to live by it.
230 says the thread and tuft are only cotton and hair; 241 says they should be cut off from the ignorant who wear them, a ruler's remedy for what 230 diagnoses.
Both say the king who fails to guard harms cows and the virtuous; the Kural gives the cost to the land (less milk, forgotten books), Tirumular the cost to the king (hell).
Both make punishing wrongdoers a king's proper work, not a stain on him; Tirumular sets it beside punishment in the next world.
Both call rain nectar (அமிழ்தம், அமுது): the Kural because the world is sustained by it, Tirumular because it makes the trees flow with nectar.
Both use the crow that calls its flock before eating: the Kural for the wealth that comes to those who keep kin close, Tirumular as a lesson in giving.
Both say to share food with all before eating, friend or not; the Naladiyar warns that the door of the other world is shut on those who shut their door and eat.

Both set the bar for giving so low no one can refuse it: the Naladiyar asks for even a fragment of a rice grain daily before eating, Tirumular a handful before eating, with a leaf for God and a kind word added.
Both make feeding those who have nothing the very form of virtue; the Kural calls it where the wealthy store their wealth, Tirumular says the learned call such food virtue itself.
Both press good deeds by picturing the deathbed: the Kural's hiccup that stops the tongue, Tirumular's fever and eyes that no longer open.
Both reject youth as a reason to put off virtue: the Naladiyar's storm drops unripe fruit, Tirumular's Death does not ask whether one is young.
Both picture a great sea to be crossed. In the Kural it is the sea of births, swum by reaching the Lord's feet; Tirumular makes it the sea of deeds, crossed in the boat of austerity and virtue.

Both compare unshared wealth to the fruit of the poisonous etti. In the Kural it ripens in the middle of town where no one can use it; in Tirumular it ripens and falls, and the usurer buries his store in the ground.
Both fault the person who watches beauty, youth and bodies pass and still does no good thing.
The Kural says the fiery disease of hunger will not touch one who shares his food; Tirumular extends the promise to cough, fever and tumour, taking literally what the Kural keeps to hunger.
Both read present fortune as the fruit of past virtue: the Kural points to the palanquin's bearer and rider, Tirumular to joy and sorrow settled by former deeds.
Both refuse gain got by leaving fairness: the Kural says to give it up the same day, Tirumular that the Lord will not let pleasure sought that way stand.

Both correct what 'the ignorant' (அறியார், அறிவிலார்) say about love: the Kural that love serves not only virtue but also against wrong, Tirumular that love is not a second thing beside Siva. Each widens love past a limit set on it.

Both join bones, burning and love. In the Kural virtue scorches the loveless as the sun a boneless worm; in Tirumular a man burns his own bones and flesh, and without love it still does not reach God.
270 says love is Siva; 279 spells out what follows: he dwells within love and is close support only to those who dwell in it.
270 says those who know love is Siva rest as that love; 287 warns that people who claim to know him through love, while blind to their own births and deaths, do not.
Both set love above attainment: 272 says self-burning austerity does not reach him without love, 284 that the siddhas never discern him while devotees receive release.
Both give the learned eyes. The Kural says the unlearned have two sores for eyes; Tirumular places an eye in the thought of the learned.
Both make learning something that goes with a person: the Kural through seven births, Tirumular as a companion, without saying how far.
Both turn attachment toward the Lord: the Kural says cling to the one free of clinging in order to let go, Tirumular says if you would cling, cling to the Supreme.
252 asks of everyone a leaf for God; 292 makes such worship of his feet the content of learning itself.
Both raise listeners to the gods: the Kural's listeners, though on earth, equal the gods fed by oblation; Tirumular's hearers of Siva's word become gods.
Both picture the moral life as walking on slippery ground. The Kural gives the words of the virtuous as a staff there; Tirumular asks the mind not to slip from listening and conduct.
Both call listening a துணை, a support. The Kural makes it a staff in faltering; Tirumular places it between the body and the mind on Siva's feet in a ladder of supports.
An image without life: the Kural likens the unlearned man's good looks to a clay doll; Tirumular makes the Lord a stone cow, giving no milk, to those who neither recite nor realise him.

Both deny learning its fruit without the Lord: the Kural asks what learning gains if one does not worship the feet of the one of pure knowledge, Tirumular calls the learned without Siva-knowledge wretches and fools.

The Kural makes learning the eyes and gives the unlearned two sores; 310, if read as it seems, gives sight to the unlearned who have the grace-eye and denies the learned their joy. The contrast depends on reading கல்லாதவர் as the book-unlearned.
The Kural finds the unlearned very good if they keep silent before the learned; Tirumular will not even look at or listen to unlearned fools, though he too grants that the merely unlearned are good.
315 mocks those who reckoned and wrote till they wore out; 316 keeps reckoning (கணக்கு) but makes the true one the only way to see. Reckoning is not rejected, only the wrong kind.

The Kural says the world won't count as ruin the low estate of one who stays fair; Tirumular promises those who stand in the middle knowledge, no hell and godhood. The same virtue, given rewards beyond this world.

Both find the fault of drinking in self-forgetting: the Kural's drinker pays to buy self-oblivion (மெய்யறியாமை), Tirumular's sectarians lose the power they sought because they forget themselves (தம்மை மறத்தல்).
325 names the nectar of bliss that comes in samadhi; 335 says how, by binding the breath to taste the moon's nectar, and sets it against liquor's loss of understanding.
The Kural simply says do not drink. Tirumular agrees, but keeps the vocabulary of drink: the clear toddy (தேறல்) he commends is Siva's bliss. Abstinence becomes a substitution.

The same phrase in two domains: in 320 those who stand in the middle (நடுவுநின்றார்) gain knowledge and godhood; in 337 the earth that does not stand level (நடுவுநில்லாது) tilts toward ruin until a sage restores it.
The Kural's fair man is a balance whose beam leans to no side; Tirumular's world, leaning to one side, is set level by Agastya. One image of rightness as balance, moral in one, cosmic in the other.
343 says the myth of the three cities is about the soul's impurities; 345 does the same for the slaying of Death, turning it into breath and fire raised in the body.
A third deed read inwardly: after the cities as impurities (343), the burning of Kama becomes the yogi's restraint of the mind and the linga's way.
Both tell Daksha's punishment by Siva: 340 the head cut and burned and restored, 353 the sacrifice broken by Siva's anger and the gods scattering.

343 calls fools those who say he burned three cities, meaning the cities are the impurities; 348 still names him the destroyer of the three cities, so the epithet stands and only its literal sense is questioned.

197 makes not killing the finest flower of worship; 351 tells, with approval shown by the reward, of a devotee who cut down his own father to protect his worship. The conflict depends on reading 351 as commending the act rather than only reporting a legend.

362 mentions in passing the two who quarrel over who is king while the Lord stands as light; 372 tells the same quarrel as the search for the head and feet of the column of fire, naming Brahma and Vishnu and their folly.
Both turn on Siva carrying a skull: 366, as tradition reads it, the head he took from Brahma; 371 the bones and skulls of the gods he bears so they won't crumble to dust.
audit_text_issue: 366 is obscure throughout; வலம்பன் in 371 may be corrupt.

note: 349 says only that Siva gave the discus to Achyuta; 368 and 369 tell how Vishnu could not bear it until he worshipped Siva, who then divided its power.
353 tells of Daksha's sacrifice breaking down at Siva's anger; 370 adds an episode from it, Vishnu turning the discus Siva gave him against Siva's side.

Both turn to skulls. The Naladiyar's skulls in the burning ground grin at the living as proof of what the body comes to; Tirumular's are borne by Siva, and his bearing them is what keeps them from becoming dust. One image teaches the body's end, the other the Lord's hold even over what is dead.

The Kural defines folly as the pride that says 'we are bright'; Tirumular shows it at the top of the cosmos, Brahma and Vishnu each saying 'I am the Lord' through folly (பேதைமை), and failing before the fire.
349 records Siva's giving the sword to Brahma and the discus to Vishnu; 379 judges such gifts: the gods who worship the giver of the sword do not reach his feet, as those who give themselves do.
Both open on circling through the aeon (ஊழி வலஞ்செய்): in 349 Brahma and Vishnu circle Siva and receive weapons, in 380 one who circles is answered as Siva outshines the sun of dissolution.

The Kural says the world has the Primal Lord as its first, as letters have 'a'; Tirumular says one alone creates, protects and removes the worlds. The Kural names only primacy; Tirumular spells it out as the three acts.

Both speak of the one who made the world. The Kural, conditionally, curses him if he meant some to live by begging; Tirumular praises him without reserve. Because the Kural's curse is conditional, this is a difference of attitude, not a contradiction.
The same quatrain twice, with ஓராயமே (one host) in place of ஒருவனுமே (one alone): if ஆயம் is the assembled powers, the second recasts the one agent as a company.
audit_text_issue: ஓராயமே may be a corruption of 404's ஒருவனுமே.

note: 386 gives creation to one He and one She with five sons; 404 to one alone. Read with 396 and 401, the She is his Shakti, so the two agree that the agent is one.
386 names the pair who create; 396 says what their creating is: play that bears fruit in every season.
382 has bindu rise from nada and the will; 1923 lists what unfolds from bindu as it rises: kundalini, the gods, the powers and speech.
Both make the bindu of Maya the source of everything: 410 by listing sun, moon, elements, speech and mind, 1930 by calling bindu the cause in all its effects, as clay in a pot.
1927 gives the five acts to the Supreme; 398 says the five lords who carry them out are born of bindu and still bound by anava. The acts are his, the agents are not.
audit_text_issue: Both verses are obscure; 1927 வீயம் may refer to bindu.

note: Both use the pot. In 1930 bindu is the clay that stays in the pot, the material cause; in 417 the Lord is the potter who shapes it. Read together they separate maker and material.

Both put the world in the pot on the fire (உலை). The Naladiyar's turtle plays in the water not knowing it is being cooked, as men revel while Death waits; Tirumular sees the whole world softened and burnt like rice, a cosmic act he says he has come to know, not a warning to the heedless.
The same four names of dissolution, defined differently: daily dissolution is sleep's stupor in 425 and shedding the two bodies in 426. Only the last, grace, stays fixed across 425 to 428.

372 has Brahma and Vishnu, each claiming lordship, searching in vain for Hara's feet; 433 says the three gods together do not know how he placed the body. The gods' ignorance of Siva is the same theme, turned here to concealment.
386 gives the world-maker five sons and calls the creator the holy one; 438 names the gods (Maheshvara, Hara, Tirumal, Ayan) as forms the one Lord becomes and works through.

Both use clay and pot. In 1930 bindu stays in the worlds as clay stays in the pot, the material cause; in 440 one clay making many vessels is the one Lord behind all wombs, who like the eye is not seen.

Kural 9 calls the one to be worshipped எண்குணத்தான், possessor of eight qualities, without naming him; Tirumular gives the eight qualities to the matted-haired Siva who keeps the world and stays near the mind.
404 repeats ஒருவனுமே: one alone made, kept and removed the worlds. 445 to 447 use the same refrain form for creation, and 447 ends, like 404's second line, with his keeping what he made.

Both see the body as a pot. In the Naladiyar it is a woman's body, a pot oozing filth that fools admire for its skin; in Tirumular it is the vessel in which the Lord's form stands like milk in water, so to see within it is bliss.

Both use milk mixed in water. The Naladiyar's swan separates them, as the wise sort what is worth learning; Tirumular's milk stays in the water, the Lord present throughout the body and seen only by steady sight.

431, opening the chapter on concealment, says the heart lives with the Lord and does not know his form; 450, closing the chapter on grace, has the poet see that form standing in the body like milk in water.
Both turn to clay. In 440 one clay making many vessels shows one Lord behind many wombs; in 443 the potter shaping clay as he wishes shows the world becoming whatever Nandi wills.
The same verse appears twice: 2926 reads ஆகிப் படைத்தன in line 2 where 457 reads மூழ்கின்ற முத்தனும், and 457's recorded variants are 2926's readings.
audit_text_issue: duplicate verse with divergent second line; one version is likely a corruption

note: Both list the body as bone, sinew and flesh. The Naladiyar asks which of these parts is the woman a man desires; Tirumular sees in the same parts a house built by the Lord and seeks its builder.

Both describe the body by its nine openings. The Naladiyar makes it a pot seeping filth and calls the man who admires it a fool; Tirumular makes the nine gates sluices set by the Lord, who dwells at its crown and is met there. The conflict is over the body's worth and depends on reading 470 as valuing the body, not only describing how it was made.
725 says Tirumular once thought the body a blemish, then found the Lord had made it his temple, and so cherishes it; 470 already finds the Lord set within the body he built.
Both use the seed or tuber and its sprout: 1932 says seed and sprout exist only together, 489 that the Lord is present as each stage of the growth.
115 states that when Pati draws near, Pasu and Pasam do not remain; 497 describes those in whom this has happened: become Siva, free of பசுபாசம், the malas destroyed.
Both make embodiment serve release: in 474 the body is fashioned so that the bond may leave the soul, in 492 Shakti and Siva yoke souls to maya so as to make them full of Siva.
Both say a small gift in worthy hands grows beyond its size: the Naladiyar's banyan seed shades the sky, Tirumular's sesame of gold yields release and siddhi.
audit_text_issue: 501 line 3 runs தரும்நிலமத் together across the line division

note: Both say which gift truly counts. The Kural makes the recipient's need the test, calling all other giving a measured loan; Tirumular makes it the recipient's knowledge of Siva, and says gifts to fools bear no fruit however large. The conflict depends on taking மூடர் as the spiritually ignorant whatever their need.
audit_text_issue: 501 lines 3-4 look misdivided and garbled (தரும் at line start; பலமும்அற் றெபர)

note: 505 continues the point from the other side: a gift to those without conduct or vows is like milking a barren cow or a crop past its season.

The converse case: the Naladiyar's small gift that reaches the hands of the worthy grows like a banyan seed until the sky looks small; Tirumular's gift to the undisciplined is a crop sown after its season. Both make the recipient's worth decide the gift's fruit.

250 tells the giver to give to everyone and not ask who they are; 506 calls giving to those without discipline and love a great fault. The two conflict if 506's ஈவது means giving in general; if it means imparting yoga teaching, they speak of different gifts.

The Kural defines true giving as giving to those who have nothing, all else being a loan expecting return; Tirumular judges the recipient by discipline and love, not by need. The conflict holds on the reading of 506 as about material giving.
The Kural's many who bathe with an air of distinction while their minds are stained, and Tirumular's deceitful who tramp from water to water: both deny that outer washing reaches the stain within.
116 says Nandi has made his home in the temple called this body; 513 draws the consequence for pilgrims, who search outside for one already inside.
510 says bathers alone cannot join the Lord; 512 lets the gods become meritorious by bathing in the Ganga. Bathing gains merit but not union, if the two are read together.

The same link between rain and worship, run in opposite directions: in the Kural, if the sky dries up, festival and worship cease even for the gods; in Tirumular, if the pujas lapse, the earth has no rain.

Both list what declines when a guardian fails: in the Kural, if the king does not guard, cows give less and Brahmins forget their books; in Tirumular, if the temple pujas stop, kings come to harm and theft grows. The king is the cause in one and the casualty in the other.
241 says that when those whose ignorance remains take up the tuft and thread, the land withers and the king loses standing; 519 says the same of a Brahmin in name only who worships in the temple.
524 makes the downward face the lower cosmos and the Lord of the aeon; 525 makes it the flower that opens a hundredfold and the endless Shakti.
229 says Brahmins who heard Vedanta and kept their craving have not truly heard it; 529 says Vedic Brahmins who dwell on pleasure forget the Lord. In both, Vedic standing is undone by desire.

Commentators read the Kural's வேந்தன் as Indra, who falls midway if those of exalted vows are angered; Tirumular names Indra's throne (வாசவன் பீடம்) and great kings' thrones as ruined when devotees are troubled.
Both start from not honouring the great (பேணாது, பேணார்); the Kural warns of ills that do not leave, Tirumular calls those who do it base.

Both use the good thing at hand left for a worse one: the ripe jackfruit for the wild date in 201, the gem for a stone and ghee and curd for bitter food in 536. One is about another man's wife, the other about leaving the guru's knowledge.
534 threatens land, kings and Indra's throne when devotees are troubled; 537 sends those who speak ill of them to low hell. One names the public ruin, the other the personal one.

The Kural asks for bearing wrongs done to one and then forgetting them; Tirumular places forbearance inward, as checking the creature of craving that grips the senses. Both call it forbearance, but the Kural's is toward others and Tirumular's toward oneself.

The Naladiyar's drain water that joins a great river becomes holy water, and the lowborn who join the good stand like a hill; Tirumular says joining the great is supreme bliss. Both make the company one joins transform the joiner.
The Kural calls cherishing the great and making them one's own the rarest of rare things; Tirumular's verse begins with அருமை and ends with 'I have joined those strong in holiness'.
543 resolves to go along with those who run to the Lord and reach his feet with them; 547 tells it happening, going with the devotees' devotees and being called in at the gate.

219 says that when the fire is worshipped and rises, the ills of deeds burn away like a wick; 551 calls sacrifice a mean path with no way through. The conflict depends on reading யாகத்திற் as the printed text has it, not the variant யாக்கத்திற்.
audit_text_issue: 551 has variant யாக்கத்திற்; 219's வீழிசெய்து is obscure

note: 552 names yama as the first limb; 554 lists what the man of yama is: one who does not kill, lie or steal, shares his food and is free of drink and lust.
The Kural puts not killing first and not lying right behind it; Tirumular's list of yama opens in the same order, கொல்லான் then பொய் கூறான்.
Both name sharing one's food (பகுத்துண்டு, பகுந்துண்பான்) among the chief virtues; the Kural sets it beside protecting all life, Tirumular makes it part of the yogi's yama.
197 makes not killing the brightest flower in the worship of the guru; 554 puts it at the head of the yogi's restraints.

557 counts sacrifice (மகம்) among the ten niyamas the yogi must keep; 551 calls the path of sacrifice a mean path with no way through. The conflict holds if 551's யாகத்திற் is read as printed; on the variant யாக்கத்திற் it vanishes.
554 lists not killing, not stealing and freedom from lust under yama; 556 repeats them under niyama with purity, compassion and forbearance. The division between the two limbs is not kept strictly.
Both say a discipline can overcome Death (கூற்று): the Kural credits the power of tapas with leaping past Death, Tirumular the measure of the held breath with kicking him.

The Naladiyar's wise renounce in childhood because grey hair will surely come; Tirumular says purified breath turns the hair black. Read literally, they disagree about whether ageing can be undone; read symbolically, 575 is not about hair, and the tension dissolves.
Both turn on twelve: 576 says the breath goes out twelve finger-breadths, and 577 makes the twelve elephants that, once known, no longer keep day and night.

The Kural asks one to draw in the five senses like a tortoise for protection through seven births; Tirumular's withdrawal goes on past restraint to what is found inside: the one the Veda searched for.
Both place the inner power two fingers above the lower opening and two below the genital one: 580 calls it kundalini, 584 only a light.
Both end with the same line, that Siva will not leave, and both make it the fruit of the breath held within.
audit_text_issue: 586 line 1 (புறப்பட்ட வாயுப் புகவிடா) is hard to construe.

note: Both use the heron that waits motionless: in the Kural it is the king biding his time before striking, in Tirumular the yogi who holds still in breath and mind.
Both say no one who came before has escaped death: the Naladiyar shows it in kings under their umbrellas, Tirumular in all who came before.
580 places the coiled kundalini at the root; 590 has the power rising from the root region roused and joined above, with the return to youth as its fruit.
Both call the yogic body a bedchamber (பள்ளி அறை): in 594 it is the great chamber with two doors where held breath lets one live long, in 611 the chamber where it is always day.
Both promise the yogi the body's survival for an aeon (ஊழி): 591 through binding the breath at the lower door, 612 through rising up the spine through the three mandalas.
Both measure the yogic body from the navel in fingers: 580 places coiled kundalini four fingers below it, 616 places the point of contemplation four fingers above.
audit_text_issue: 616 நடலித்த, மடலித்த, கடலித்து may be corrupt.

note: 552 lists the eight limbs from yama to samadhi; 618 draws the consequence that samadhi is reached only through yama and the rest, so the ethical limbs are the way to the highest.
618 makes samadhi the fruit of the limbs; 631 says that for one who goes with the Lord samadhi is not needed and for one who becomes him there is none, so the chapter's goal is itself relative.
583 calls closing the lower door and fixing the mind on the upper one the way to conquer time; 622 says that once the upper door opens Death's word is not heard even in dreams.
The Kural says those who have won the power of austerity can even leap past Death; Tirumular names a yogic means, the upper door seen open, for the same escape.

The Naladiyar says no one here has leapt clear of Death and escaped, so give your wealth now; Tirumular says the yogi who sees the upper door will not hear Death even in dreams. The conflict holds on the literal reading of 622, that the yogi escapes death; if it means only freedom from fear of death, it dissolves.

604 sets the two gazes at the middle of the nose and lists what ceases, seeking (தேட்டம்) among them; 624 turns the gaze back to the eye and settles the breath in the ground 'without seeking' (தேட்டற்ற), and names the fruit.

Both speak of the one who goes upon the flower and of those who reach his feet. The Kural promises they live long upon the earth (or, as Parimelazhagar takes it, in the world of release); Tirumular promises Amaravati, then in the following verses the Siva-state.

597 defines dharana as holding with the Supreme (தரித்தது தாரணை தற்பரத்தோடே) after dissolving body into elements and mind; 639 defines samadhi as joining the Supreme (தற்பரஞ் சேர்தல்) after going beyond all upadhi. The two limbs differ as holding and joining.
585 makes pratyahara the separating and dissolving of upadhi from the inner light; 639 makes samadhi the going beyond upadhi altogether, so the two verses mark stages on one line.
audit_text_issue: Both verses are technical and partly obscure (639 தாரியல்).

note: Both say a discipline can carry one past Death: the Kural's power gained through tapas leaps over Yama (கூற்றம் குதித்தல்); Tirumular's yogis of the brow and staff have no Yama (நமனில்லை).

The Naladiyar says no one has leapt clear of Death and escaped, so give while you can; Tirumular says those who know the yogic way have no Yama. The conflict holds if நமனில்லை means escape from bodily death; if it means freedom from Yama's judgement after death, the two need not clash.

The Naladiyar's wise renounce in childhood because grey hair will surely come; Tirumular says that by the eighth stage of practice grey hair and wrinkles do not appear. The conflict depends on reading 647 literally, as a claim about the body, and not as a figure for inner freshness.

Both say not every lamp is the lamp: the Kural's one true lamp is truthfulness, Tirumular's is the higher inner light that makes release easy. The image is shared, the light is moral in one and yogic in the other.
669 says the eight siddhis come by eightfold yoga and mastered breath; 670 adds that they come into being only when Shakti Tripurai grants grace. Technique is necessary but not sufficient.
Two lists of the eight siddhis in one chapter. 668's is closer to the standard anima list; set side by side they show the items were not fixed in wording.
audit_text_issue: 649 has known variants (நோன்மையும், ககனமும்); 668's நேர்மை / இணுகாத வேகார் uncertain

note: 641 credits the siddhis and the end of birth to grace given to one who sought the Lord's feet; 707 says outward travel finds nothing, and love alone knows where the Lord dwells.

The same charge in two parts of the yogic body: no one knows how the breath is wasted (அழியும் படியை அறிகிலர், 720), people do not know how much bindu is lost (1936). In both the knowing is the remedy: 720 says the one who learns it can join the breath to Nandi.

On what the body is worth: the Naladiyar calls it a pot seeping filth from nine openings, attractive only through its skin, and the man who praises it a fool; Tirumular says he once held the body base (இழுக்கு) but found the Lord had made it his temple, and so cherishes it. The conflict holds if the Naladiyar's verse is read as a verdict on the body and not only as a remedy for lust.

Both value the body for what it yields, but the Naladiyar has the body thrown away like crushed cane once its juice is taken, while Tirumular says the body must be nurtured because life and true knowledge perish with it.

Both rest on the three humours of the medical writers, wind among them: the Kural says excess or lack of them brings disease, Tirumular names the time of day at which practice removes each, and promises the end of age as well.
The Kural says that eating in measure is how one who has a body keeps it long; Tirumular counts the reduction of food among the means of perfecting the body.
Both claim that Death can be overcome: the Kural by the power gained through austerity, Tirumular by seeing the Lord's feet in the inner fire before Death strikes.
Both make time the quiet cutter of life: the Kural's day is a saw for those who understand it, Tirumular's naazhigai run out while people know everything else.
Both say that discipline can carry a person past death: the Kural credits the power of austerity, Tirumular the ability to seek the Siva-state within.
Both analyse Om into A, U and M; 1926 adds bindu and nada's end, 765 places M in the inner channel where the Lord settles.
762 says the unpassing thing is found by looking within the passing; 786 says no one knows the perishing thing, and that the poet has come to know the knowing.
724 says Tirumular learned how to nourish the body and so the life; 758 takes the claim to its limit, the yogi's body kept a thousand years and more.

Both make the body a temporary dwelling: the Kural's life has only borrowed shelter in it, Tirumular's body is a fair hut the Lord has shaped. The Kural laments the lack of a home; Tirumular looks to loosening the bond of the old dwelling.
741 says people perish without noticing their time run out; 786 names what measures it, fire and breath, and claims the knowledge others lack.

The Naladiyar counts those who prattle astrology among the greatest fools, beside those who neglect their real task; Tirumular sets weekday omens inside a yoga tantra. Whether this is a true conflict depends on whether the Naladiyar's சோதிடம் includes such day lore or means endless study that displaces the work of release.
Both end on the same words, நட்டம் இருக்க நமனில்லை: in 574 after holding the breath by measure, in 799 after sealing the body for khechari. Tirumular gives the same promise to two practices.

The Kural says those who have gained the power of austerity can even leap past Death; Tirumular says Yama has no hold on the yogi who seals the body. Both make death conquerable, the Kural by austerity in general, Tirumular by a named technique.
The same closing lines, grey hair and wrinkles undone and the yogi made a child by Nandi's command, follow two different means: union with a woman in 734, the breath set in the palate in 805.
audit_text_issue: 805: ந்யாலம் is a corruption of ஞாலம்.

note: 725 says Tirumular once held the body worthless, then found the Lord's temple inside it; 820 shows how that temple is lit, with held breath as its gem lamp.

Both call the body a bag (பை). The Naladiyar says it should be looked at as a bag turned inside out, a covered foulness to be shunned; Tirumular says that inside the same bag a light shines and it becomes a temple. The conflict holds if 820's பை is read as the body, as tradition takes it.

The Kural asks what worth is if one does not do sweet things even to those who harm one. Tirumular's inward yogis are good even to the hostile, but worse than fire to doers of evil, so their goodness has a limit the Kural's does not state.
Both use the weekday planets. In 790 வெள்ளி and பொன் name Friday and Thursday in a rule for the breath; in 826 and 836 the same words become silver and gold, a code for the bindu and the body.
1936 laments that people neither know how much bindu is lost nor how to guard it; 828 gives one answer: guard it in union itself, so that the very act that spends it keeps it.

Both make union life-giving. In the Kural the lover feels his life put out shoots at each touch, as if her shoulders were ambrosia; in Tirumular union practised as yoga lets one live on earth for many ages. Love's hyperbole in one is a technique in the other.
Both promise the end of grey hair and wrinkles (நரைதிரை) from a bodily practice: 727 from breath held at fixed hours, 848 from drinking the shore-water the witless shun.

The Naladiyar treats grey hair as certain to come, so the wise renounce in childhood; Tirumular says that for those who drink this water grey hair and wrinkles change and Yama is absent. The conflict holds if 848 is read literally of the body, not as a figure for spiritual youth.
audit_text_issue: 848 வரைவரை and the identity of the water (amuri) are obscure

note: 1936 faults people who do not know how bindu is lost or how to guard it; 877 describes the yogi in whom bindu does not go out, held at the base for want of desire.
724 says that if the body perishes life perishes, so Tirumular learned to nourish the body; 879 gives the condition for their not parting: awareness and body kept in balance.
Both use the moon's two fortnights: the Kural for friendship with the good that fills and with fools that wanes, Tirumular for the inner moon whose growing and shrinking the yogi must learn.

Both use the eclipse serpent that seizes the moon: the Naladiyar's spares the young crescent, as the worthy spare a fallen enemy; Tirumular's enmity of serpent and moon is ended and the two held together, an inner joining.

The Kural says only those who reach the Lord's feet cross the sea of births; 905 promises no further birth to whoever chants the five letters, and 898 has already made the Lord's feet the letters. The means is narrowed from the feet to the mantra that is the feet.

Both free a person from deeds through the Lord's name: the two kinds of deed do not cling to those who delight in his true praise (Kural), and subtle karma is destroyed by chanting the subtle mantra (909). Tirumular adds a count and a technique.

115 names Pati, Pasu and Pasam and says Pasu and Pasam do not stand when Pati draws near; 895 names the three impurities (anava, maya, karma) and sets the stainless dance among them, on the traditional reading that the dance is where they end.

In 589 the holy dance goes on in a hall reached by a waterfall through the long nadi, an image usually read as inside the body; 886 names the outer hall at Chidambaram. Together they show the hall Tirumular means is both.
725 turns from despising the body to cherishing it as the Lord's temple; 906 goes further and promises that the mantra makes the capable one's body gold.
Both use the letter A to point beyond itself. The Kural makes A, first of letters, the image of the Primal Lord first in the world; Tirumular makes A the soul and gives the Supreme to U.
Both put a goad over 'the five'. In the Kural it is firmness of mind (உரன்) that guards the five; in Tirumular the five elephants in the forest are goaded by the five syllables.
Both make control of the five senses the way in: the Naladiyar's one who steers the craving of the five gates reaches release, Tirumular's one who holds the five together lets the First enter.
Both say deeds lose their hold on one devoted to the Lord: the Kural through his true praise, Tirumular through his name kept up without tiring, with the Lord coming to remove the grief of deeds.
Both define the Brahmin by something other than birth, if 940 is read that way: the Kural by kindness to all life, Tirumular by the five syllables dwelling in him.
The same verse recurs in the ninth tantra's gross pancakshara, with 'once the order of the fifty is known' for 'once what the fifty become is known'.
A near-doublet in the Bhairavi mantra chapter; there the lady herself departs and cuts away the babble, here the speaker does.
audit_text_issue: tm:1115 line 1 மேலி is probably a corruption of மேவி.

note: Both make the recited syllables drive out the impurities: here the three malams flee crying out, in 2712 sivaya removes all impurity and yields Siva-jnana yoga.
885 builds a ladder of one, two and three letters from the one letter that becomes the world; 962 says the six letters must be recited as one, and that by one letter life is won.
Both use the alchemist's pill (குளிகை) that makes gold: here the realised true object is the pill like purified gold, in 2709 sivayanama is the pill that turns the body's cage to gold.
Both move the temple inward: 1823 makes the body a shrine and the heart the great temple, 919 makes the five syllables and the subtle within the temple where the Lord sits.
audit_text_issue: 919 obscure (தூலம்/சூக்குமம் may be body or mantra)

note: 958 mocks those who perform the twilight rite without knowing the mantra within; 978 says those who join with Shakti at the root need no rite at all.
Near-doublets: the same breath-joined recitation with O, ending on 'the first Lord MA', one starting from NA and one from SI.

198 sends those who say 'kill, strike' bound to hell; 1000 gives a rite for killing by mantra and diagram. The conflict holds if 1000 is read as offering the rite for use; read as a catalogue of what mantra can do, it is a report, not an endorsement.
1003 to 1006 prescribe flowers, pastes and lamps and promise every fruit; 1008 says the Lord's servants, the Siva-yogis and the desireless do not want such ritual work, only love.
1012 places the mantra's syllables in the body; 1013 says what the parts of நமசிவாய stand for: நம the bound soul, சிவ the Lord.

Both promise the end of sorrow to those who come to the Lord's feet; Tirumular reaches it through worship with lamps and offerings, the Kural through reaching the feet of the one without liking or aversion.
The Kural praises the path of the one who quenched the five senses; Tirumular says those who seek through the senses (பொறிவழி) only lament, and the Lord is found within.
1030 and the verses around it give the Lord counted feet, faces and eyes in the fire; 1031 says the endless one has no place, no measure and no word that reaches him. The forms are aids, not limits.
724 says Tirumular learned to nurture the body so as to nurture life; 1042 says those who guarded the body and dwelt within it lived through a crore of ages.
Both say deeds cannot cling to the one turned to the Lord: the Kural through his true praise, Tirumular through seeing the fire rise within.

Both name Mahamaya and speech among the first powers; in 1925 they shine within bindu, in 1045 they and the bindu-born (வயிந்தவம்) are all forms of one Tripura. The bindu chapter's cosmology here gets a goddess's face.

Both make the Goddess the one who unfolds as nada and bindu: 1048 has Tripura grant nada and nada's end while the supreme bindu becomes the worlds, 1138 has Sivashakti spread out as bindu and nada within the mind.
Both portraits give the Goddess the noose and goad. Tripura (1049) adds the sugarcane bow and flower arrows; Bhairavi (1081) adds the trident and skull. Same emblems, gentle and fierce forms.

1053 says no god fails to know her and nothing the five do is done without her; 1087 says the many gods, Siva, Brahma and Vishnu among them, look to the Lady as cause. Both put the Goddess behind every god.
1066 has her stand as his body and life; 1137 says the lady and he stand in one form and people do not see it. Both deny any gap between Siva and Shakti.

The Kural calls a head that does not bow at the feet of the Lord of eight qualities as useless as a sense that cannot sense; Tirumular tells the head to wear the Goddess's feet and the mouth to praise her. The same claim for the head, turned to the Goddess.

The Kural traces joyless birth to the delusion (மருள்) that takes what is not real as real (பொருள்). Tirumular uses the same pair: the Goddess turns the deluded mind into one that has found the true thing, so grace is the remedy for the Kural's diagnosis.

The chapter opens with Bhairavi as the first of twelve kalas, a count in a mantra, and closes with her as the first of the twelve again; by the end the count is a name of the goddess praised as beginning and beginningless.
1106 leaves the maiden asleep in the middle channel; 1107 has Manonmani come in sleep, embrace and say 'do not sleep'. Read together, the waking is hers and his at once.
1118 ends calling maya darkness; 1119 opens by saying darkness is Shakti and light is the Lord, so the darkness is not rejected but given to her as one of two powers.
audit_text_issue: 1118 line 2 is corrupt (துன்னியங fகைவரைப் has a stray character)

note: 1115 says she cut away the poet's babble with the five-syllable mantra; 1116 says the foolish who went on babbling passed away, while she stands before those whose effort is complete.
The same line of names (woman, samadhi, Manonmani, the auspicious one) in both; in 1114 she joins the heart, in 1120 she blossoms in it, a refrain that marks the hymn's stages.
Both make reaching or bowing at the divine feet the end of births: the Kural's sea of births, Tirumular's cruel births. Tirumular gives it to the goddess, the Kural to the unnamed Lord.
The Kural says the two kinds of deed do not cling to those who praise the Lord truly; 1122 praises her by name after name and ends that she drove out the poet's deeds.

The two verses share a frame (தார்மேல்/தாமேல் உறைவிடம், பார்மேல், பூமேல் உறைகின்ற ... வந்தனள்): 1130 fills it with Brahma and the goddess of speech, 1141 with the lotus petals and the bangled lady. They may be variants of one verse.
audit_text_issue: 1141 line 2 (இதழ்பழி னெட்டிரு நூறுன) looks garbled; 1130's ஒரு நூறு is unexplained

note: Both make the goddess and bindu one: 1925 sets Mahamaya, the goddess of speech and kundalini within bindu, 1138 has Shakti spread out as bindu and nada.

Both cut a pride (செருக்கு) voiced as possession: the Kural's 'I' and 'mine', Tirumular's 'my mother, my father' said of the divine parents. Tirumular extends the Kural's renunciation of ownership to the soul's claim on God.
audit_text_issue: 1129 line 3 has a stray Latin letter: உரைசெய்Yயும்.

note: Both set love (அன்பு) against bone (என்பு). For the Kural a body without love is bone wrapped in skin; Tirumular has the father reached through love and the mother present in the bone within bondage. The pairing depends on reading என்பிற் as 'in the bone'.

Both join penance, power and the defeat of death: the Kural says those who gain the power (ஆற்றல்) of austerity can leap past death; Tirumular's goddess of rare penance stands in his power (ஆற்றல்) and drives Death (கூற்றம்) away.

Both make learning the start of a way that ends in seeing the true: the Kural's learners who see the true thing (மெய்ப்பொருள்) take the road of no return; Tirumular's learn what is to be learned, then pass through yoga and knowledge to see the Supreme.

Both say those who saw Nadanta are unwavering (நாதாந்தங் கண்டோர் நடுக்கற்ற). 1422 sets Vedanta and Siddhanta side by side; 1435 distinguishes what the seers of Vedanta, of Nadanta and of Siddhanta each hold.
audit_text_issue: TM 1422 புதாந்த likely for பூதாந்த; மாதுப் புனஞ்செய்ய obscure.

note: 1423 commends earrings, seals and beads for those of service and rite; 1438 says the pure Saiva goes beyond outward garb (வேடம் கடந்து), without show. The signs are fitting at one stage and passed beyond at another.

115 states that pasu and pasam cannot reach the Lord; 1436 repeats the line and gives it images, clouds that never reach the sky and sights that never reach the eye. It leaves out 115's other half, that when the Lord approaches they cease.
115 sets out Pati, Pasu and Pasam as beginningless; 1432 makes that triad, with impurity and release, the matter the pure Saiva contemplates.
63 names the nine Agamas Nandi received (Karanam, Kamikam and the rest); 1429 begins from the same nine before naming the twenty-eight.
1420's pure Saiva discerns the real, the unreal and what is both, and keeps clear of the sentient and the insentient; 1431's has passed beyond them, into a state where they are no longer told apart.
Both make the feet the way: in the Kural reaching the Lord's feet takes one across the sea of births; in Tirumular going by the feet of the Supreme power one becomes Siva.

The Kural says the senses must be crushed as part of renouncing; Tirumular says the five, hard to curb, subside once the truth beyond speech is attained. The same subduing is a task in one and a result in the other.
Both cut the bonds of desire by turning to the Lord: the Kural by clinging to the one without clinging, Tirumular by going to Siva's side and crushing ஆசாபாசம்.
The Kural ends the pride of 'I' and 'mine' between a person and his goods; Tirumular ends the speech of 'I' and 'He' between the soul and the Lord. Both close with the 'I' given up.
1445 ends the pilgrim's search with the Lord taking the heart as his temple; 1823 builds the whole temple inside: heart as shrine, body as temple, mouth as gate, the soul as linga.
Both make Nandi the giver of the paths: in 1449 he sets the four paths for deluded men, in 1478 he lays down the guru-path so that those on earth may be saved.
Both make the Lord's feet the only crossing of a sea: the Kural's great sea of births, Tirumular's leaping sea of deeds. Reaching the feet is the condition in both.
Both set one abstention above a mass of offerings: the Kural puts not killing and eating above a thousand fire sacrifices, Tirumular puts giving up flesh above crores of sandal and flowers.
199 threatens meat-eaters with hell; 1452 adds that their worship, however rich, does not reach the Lord's feet.
272 says even burning one's bones as firewood wins nothing without melting in love; in 1456 the devotee melts in love and the Lord shines within the bones.
375 tells how Hari and Brahma went to the crown and the foot and could not reach him; 1458 recalls their ages of striving and places him in the crown, perceived only by those who perceive.
audit_text_issue: 1458's ஒருச்சி is likely a corruption of உச்சி

note: The same four grades, samaya, visesha, nirvana and abhisheka, are initiations in 1450 and stages of yoga in 1466.

The Kural says those who learn and know the truth here do not come back; Tirumular says letters, songs and the sixty-four arts do not remove birth, and only the yogic way does. The difference may lie in what each means by learning.

The Kural asks what gain is greater than aram, which yields distinction and wealth; Tirumular says no path of aram is higher than jnana. They conflict only if the Kural's aram is meant to rank above liberating knowledge; Tirumular keeps aram but places it below jnana.
Both set the cutting off of 'I' and 'mine' at the summit: the Kural says whoever cuts that pride enters a world above the gods', Tirumular makes it jnana within jnana itself.
Both free the one who knows or praises the Lord from both kinds of deed: the Kural's twofold deeds of darkness do not cling to him, Tirumular's knower has passed beyond merit and sin alike.
The same four grades are applied to yoga and to jnana; yoga's summit is siddhi (1466), jnana's is the good guru's feet (1476).
Both promise victory over death to those of disciplined practice: the Kural to those who have gained the power of tapas, Tirumular to Siva-yoga siddhas who have put away anger.

Both make clear knowledge of what is the condition of ending birth: the Kural's mind that has examined and known what is real need not think of another birth; Tirumular says those without clarity do not end their births.
audit_text_issue: Kural 357 reads உணரான் in the base text; the commentators' உணரின் is needed for the sense.

note: 2406 says that when the soul's bound nature is removed and its bonds cut, souls cling to their Lord; 1486 calls that removal and joining sanmarga, and adds the melting heart.

631 says samadhis are not needed for one who goes with the Lord and there is no samadhi once one becomes Him; 1490 praises yoga-samadhi as holding space, light and Shakti. Samadhi is honoured as a means and set below union.

Both arm the mind against the five senses: the Kural's goad of firmness guards them like elephants, Tirumular's sharp sword of the mind cuts them down. The Kural guides the five; Tirumular strikes them.

Both make reaching the Lord's feet the crossing of a sea. The Kural names the great sea of births; Tirumular names only the shore, four times over, and makes it both the shade of the feet and the Lord's command.

The Kural calls a head that does not bow to the Lord's feet as useless as a sense that cannot sense; Tirumular says bowing and serving at Hara's feet is the very fruit of birth. One states the loss, the other the gain.
Both make the Lord answer worship itself: 1500 says he comes forth each time one worships, 1505 that he stands held by the great love of those who make him their eye.
1496 counts worship and recitation as the faultless good son's path; 1506 says the same acts, done by a mind like a stone in moss, do not know the Lord. The acts are necessary, not sufficient.

Both set the quarrel of 'this one or that one is supreme' against seeking the Lord himself: here by the ordained way of service, in 1545 by leaving the delusion of those who praise one sect over another.
725 finds that the Highest has made the body his temple; 1508 makes the worshipper's own mind the temple in kiriyai. Both move the shrine inside the person.
1507 matches the states of release to the paths; 1509 ranks the same states by what happens to the bond in each, ending in its dissolving.
audit_text_issue: 1509's சிரமானது and 1507's பாலோகம் இல்லா are doubtful readings

note: Both make lesser things gain worth by nearness: in the Naladiyar the hare is worshipped with the moon, and the slight gain worth through friends steady as a hill; in Tirumular all that nears the golden mountain turns its colour, and the disciple takes the Lord's form.

1518 repeats 1514's line, 'removing blindness and showing many good qualities', but with the Lord as the doer where 1514 had the old woman, and adds that he cut away deeds and gave knowledge. It unlocks part of the riddle: the woman's act is the Lord's.

Both use the lamp entering a dark room. The Naladiyar makes it austerity before which sin cannot stand, and warns the dark returns when the oil runs out; Tirumular makes it the Lord and the Mother entering delusion, with no warning that the light fails.

Both treat good and bad deeds alike as what must be overcome, not good deeds as a ladder. The Kural says the two dark deeds do not cling to those who praise the Lord truly; Tirumular says grace descends when the two stand in balance.
725 says the Highest has made the body his temple; 1530 faults the six sects for not seeing the God who stands within the body. The doctrine of 725 becomes the charge against the sects.
1530 says the sects miss the God within the body; 1547 says that once one knows how to reach the light standing within, the quarrel among sects ends of itself.

The Kural calls understanding seeing the true thing in whatever thing, of whatever kind; Tirumular tells people to drop the claim that this or that sect is good and seek the God beyond the forms. Both look past the label to the thing.

Both name the Lord as the one without equal and make reaching him the cure for the mind: the Kural's தனக்குவமை இல்லாதான் removes the mind's anxiety, Tirumular's துணையிலி is reached by the mind that draws near.
329 calls those held by the mala of deluding sects great fools; 1556 says those who never leave their sect die before reaching freedom from birth. Both treat staying in a sect as the obstacle.
Both mock sectarian ranking with the image of one city: 1558's six roads and barking dog, 1568's Nandi laughing at those who name 'this penance, that penance' while all who understand enter the city.
1556 condemns those who stay inside their sect and perish; 1558 says all six sects lead to one city. The road is not the fault; refusing to go beyond it, or attacking the others, is.
Both make worship of the feet the fruit of knowing: the Kural asks what learning has achieved without it, Tirumular says his examining succeeded where the gods' failed because it ended in worship.

Both use seed and sprout. 1932 makes them the inseparable cause and effect that reveal Hara's way; 1585 makes devotion and dispassion the seed and release-knowledge the sprout, which Shakti's grace makes grow.
1576 argues that the guru is pure Siva because the one beyond the worlds comes here and saves; 1581 states it flatly on Nandi's word and adds that people fail to grasp it.

The Kural asks what learning has achieved if it doesn't lead to the Lord's feet; Tirumular says even the knowledge of Vedanta cannot be known unless the Lord comes as guru. Learning is not enough in either, but for Tirumular the grace must come first.

Both are four-line anaphoras on திருவடி. 138 makes the feet Sivam, Sivaloka, the path and the refuge; 1598 makes knowledge of the feet the agent that makes one Siva, brings to Sivaloka, frees from mala and is release.

Both use the same words for the end state: beyond word (உரையற்று), without waves (திரையற்ற), shoreless (கரையற்ற). 134 describes those who understand the teacher's word; 1593 is the speaker's own passing beyond words.
Both narrate the guru placing his feet on the speaker's head: in 113 as a guard that melts him and removes the verdigris, in 1597 so that the path back to the womb is drained.
Both join the head to the Lord's feet: the Kural calls a head that does not bow to them useless, Tirumular says the old sages set the feet on their heads.
Both say the two deeds, good and bad, cease for one devoted to the Lord: the Kural through praising him, Tirumular through holding his feet in the mind.
Both make a death of the self the way to become Siva: 1907's living who have died to the three malas, 1595's speaker made Siva and made to die in the bliss beyond speech.
Both make silence the mark of the finished state: 1611 says silence brings release and powers, 1634 that chant and sound are no longer needed once samadhi is in hand.

Both set a light against darkness in the soul. The Naladiyar's lamp is a person's own tapas, which drives out sin until its oil runs out; Tirumular's light is Siva's grace that comes to the renounced soul at its ripe time.
Both put the full renouncer above the heavens: the Kural says he who cuts 'I' and 'mine' enters a world higher than the gods', Tirumular that only he who renounces the earth reaches the Lord's state.
Both put the ascetic beyond death: the Kural says those who gain the power of tapas can leap past Death, Tirumular that for those who have withdrawn and let go, Yama is simply not there.
The Kural commends tapas because whatever one wants is gained as one wants it. Tirumular separates getting what one wants, which mere asking achieves, from tapas, whose greatness is ending birth.
Both define the ascetic by firmness under pressure: the Naladiyar's blessed push aside troubles that would break their vows, Tirumular's stay unblinking amid kings at war.

Both set inner work against learned talk: the Naladiyar calls those who prattle of grammar and astrology the greatest fools, Tirumular tells the reader to leave clever shastra-recitation for a moment's inward look.

1632 says tapas falls away once the samadhi of knowledge is reached; 1644 adds a second way past it, fellowship with those already in Siva's bliss, and names the end both serve: the mind becoming Siva.
Both tie want to the lack of tapas: the Kural says the poor are many because few practise austerity, Tirumular pictures those without tapas or learning whirling around for rice.
Both picture those who do no tapas as shut out and reduced to want: in the Naladiyar they cling to the outer door of others' houses, in Tirumular they run from crocodile to bear in search of rice.

The Kural asks for flawless learning followed by living by it; Tirumular says recitation (ஓதல்) is no longer needed once the Life of life is within. The two speak of different stages, so this limits learning rather than contradicting it.

Both make அருள் the wealth above wealth. The Kural's அருள் is compassion toward living beings, and its chapter is named அருளுடைமை; Tirumular takes the same chapter name for the Lord's grace, the source of wealth, knowledge and divinity.
1625 says that only those with the Lord's grace know what tapas is; 1645 widens the claim: knowledge of every kind, with wealth and greatness, comes from grace.

Both say that both kinds of deed, good as well as bad, must cease to cling, and both tie this to the Lord: the Kural to those who love his true praise, Tirumular to seeking his dwelling beyond the two.
The Kural says cling to the one without clinging in order to let clinging go; Tirumular vows not to let go of Nandi until release, a clinging that is the way out.
Both condemn those who live by others while posing as renouncers: the Kural calls none more hard-eyed than they, Tirumular says the show of devotion they put on for food finds no feet of Siva.
241 says the land withers when the unawakened take up tuft and thread and that it is good to cut them off; 1656 repeats the harm, adding famine, and calls stripping the garb of the base a joy.
audit_text_issue: 1656 'பஞ்ச்மாம்' is a typo for பஞ்சமாம்; 'ஞானமில் லேர்' is odd.

note: Both put the world's welfare on the ruler's daily scrutiny (நாள்தோறும் நாடுக, நாடி நாடோறும): the Kural of those who do his work, Tirumular of all his people's conduct.
240 says the garb is true only for those who keep its way; 1660 restates the distinction of false and true garb and puts the test in knowledge.

Both say austerity's garb belongs only to those who already have austerity, and set தவம் against அவம்: for the Kural taking it up without it is futile, for Tirumular those great in futility cannot carry it.
audit_text_issue: kural:262 in the packet reads 'ஆகும் அதனை'; the standard text is 'ஆகும் அவமதனை', so the அவம் the note relies on is missing here.

note: Both make the false ascetic a hunter: in the Kural one hiding in a bush to snare birds, in Tirumular a வேடர் who wears the garb to kill, punning on the word for garb-wearer.

Nearly the same verse: 230 asks whether thread and tuft are Brahman and says the real thread is Vedanta and the real tuft knowledge; 1665 repeats this and adds Om as the means of seeing the supreme soul.
240 says the garb is the true garb for those who keep its way; 1668 goes further, that the knower is released even without it, so the garb is not needed at all where knowledge is.
The same move in another field: the Naladiyar says the beauty of hair and garment is not beauty and learning's is; Tirumular says garb does not save and knowledge does.

Both say the ascetic's outward marks are not needed: the Kural, neither shaving nor long hair if one gives up what the world condemns; Tirumular, no garb if one reins in the running horse and seeks Nandi.
Both make self-control the handling of animals: the Kural's goad of firmness guards the five senses as elephants, Tirumular's firm reins hold the running horse.
1660 says a garb saves only the knower; 1677 gives the reason: the garb is put on the body and falls away with it, so it cannot belong to the soul.
1680 shows the unripe choosing a teacher who cannot remove blindness and falling with him; 1693 gives the remedy: if you take a guru, take a good one, and give him body, life and goods.
Both condemn the split between word and deed: the Kural calls the bond with such people bitter even in a dream, Tirumular warns against saying one thing, thinking another and doing a third.
Both make the king's harsh punishment of the wicked a protection of the land: the Kural likens it to weeding the young crop, Tirumular says without it the earth falls to famine.
Both tie the land's famine to tolerating the wrong people: in 1656 the ignorant who wear the garb, in 1684 the sinners the king fails to drive out.
Both use the shadow that clings to the feet and never leaves: in the Kural it is the ruin that follows the evildoer, in Tirumular the true disciple's place at the guru's feet.

1823 calls the body the Lord's temple for those who have seen clearly; 1701 calls it a prison the teacher shows the disciple how to escape. The two can stand together if the body is a prison to the unreleased and a temple to the knower, but the images pull apart.

The same verse appears twice. 1492's last line reads சாதா ரணங்கெட லாஞ்ச மார்க்கமே, which supports reading 1707's as 'this is the companion's path' (சகமார்க்கம்) rather than a statement about one person.
audit_text_issue: 1707 has காலந்தத்து for கலாந்தத்து, and 1492's last line சாதா ரணங்கெட லாஞ்ச மார்க்கமே looks garbled (likely கெடலாம் சகமார்க்கமே).

note: Nearly the same verse in a later tantra: the sixteen-petalled flower and pure knowledge becoming Siva's bliss. 2359 ends with the Lord united there, 1711 with knowledge ripening, so the second differs in who is the subject.
1712 says the world has taken form as the linga; 1725 shows it in worship, with the earth as Shakti's base, the sky as the linga, the sea as its bath and the stars as its garland.

Both say the Lord took up the body as his temple (கோயில் கொண்டான்). In 725 that discovery turns Tirumular from scorning the body to caring for it; in 1722 it follows from the Lord being beyond all knowing.

2104 declares one kulam and one God; 1721 still gives each varna its own linga. The oneness of 2104 does not, in this chapter, remove ritual distinctions by birth, though 1721 claims no difference in worth.

On what the human body is: the Naladiyar breaks it into entrails, fat, blood, bone and sinew and asks which part is the beautiful woman; Tirumular says the body's very form is the Sivalinga, Chidambaram and Siva's dance. The conflict holds if the Naladiyar's verse is read as a verdict on the body and not only as a remedy for desire.
1823, in the chapter on Siva worship, makes the heart the temple, the body the shrine and the soul the linga; 1726 goes further and makes the body's own form the linga.

Both speak of the five senses as gates (வாயில்) to be mastered. The Kural praises the one who quenched the five sense-gates and the long life of those who follow him; Tirumular has Nandi enter the body by its gates and receive worship once the senses are put behind.
1726 says the human body's form is the Sivalinga, Sadasiva and the dance; 1750 says it of one's own body (தன்மேனி) and goes on to Siva-bliss and the Supreme itself.

Both start from the letter A. The Kural compares: as A comes first among letters, the Primal Lord comes first for the world; Tirumular makes the Lord himself the letter A, with Shakti as U, and the two become the earth and sound. The simile becomes an identity.
Both analyse Om into A, U and M with bindu and nada. 1926 places them in the ascent of the kalas; 1752 maps them onto the parts of the linga.

Both open with A as first: the Kural uses it as a simile, as A is first of letters so the Lord is first of the world. Tirumular takes the letter literally: A and U, known rightly, are themselves the lingam.
1754 makes bindu the first pedestal and the union the lingam; 1757 names the parts plainly, bindu as pedestal and nada as lingam, and gives the pair the five acts.
Both end on the Lord dwelling in the speaker's mind; 1762 adds the contrast with the gods who seek him outwardly across the eight directions.

1764 counts four forms, four formless and one in the middle without naming them; 1776 names nine: Brahma, Vishnu, Rudra, Mahesa, the five-faced one, bindu, nada, Shakti and Siva, and calls them the lingam.
Both make Shakti with Siva the தாபரம்: 1755 of the installed lingam, 1772 of everything fixed, with no other.
1773 says the Lord is too vast to be walked round; 1774 answers that water, flowers and his name, with knowing, are the way to circle him.
Both describe the same rite: taking body, wealth and life, setting the feet and cutting the clinging; 1783 adds the power of grace and jnana and the guru becoming one with the disciple.
In 1594 the guru takes hold of the soul's three forms and takes the disciple to save him; 1784 makes the same taking of life, wealth and body, and adds that what he took was his own gift.
Both make the guru's hand on the disciple the moment of release: in 1590 the red guru places his hand on the head; in 1778 he places hand and feet and shows the way out of birth.
Both call a failure of understanding ghostly: the Kural's man who denies what the world holds to be is counted a demon, Tirumular's who don't know how body, breath and soul join are like ghosts.
